p.t: In short

A demo store is a **test shop** with stand-in products. Build it before you contact any supplier.
Keep it small: about **5** demo products is the target. 10 to 20 is the upper limit.
Use free photos **labeled for reuse**. Never copy supplier or competitor photos before approval.
Use your own **domain name** (your own web address). Never use a store-name.myshopify.com address in outreach.
When the store goes live, **replace** every demo product with an approved supplier product.

**Demo products** are sample items for showing suppliers. They are never for sale.
Use **your own domain name** (your own web address), not the free Shopify address.

**Remove the password** and keep payments off until real supplier products are ready.
**Replace** demo products with real supplier products as soon as the first supplier approves.
What a supplier-ready demo store is
A demo store is a fully working **Shopify (online shop software) storefront (the shop front customers see) with**
**placeholder (stand-in) products. It is "supplier-ready," meaning ready for brands to approve. It is not connected to approved suppliers and does not accept real customer orders.**
**It becomes a live store later, when the demo products are replaced** with approved supplier products.
It has a complete layout and design, filled with a **small number** of representative (typical) demo products.
Suppliers review it to picture how their own products would look before they approve real uploads.
It is built to be supplier-ready. It looks and behaves like a live store (a store open for real sales).
The **finished design** is used to show brands when applying to become an authorized retailer (a store a brand allows to sell its products).

It should be built **exactly like the permanent store, with the same design and pages. The only difference is that the real products stay unpublished** (hidden from customers) until the supplier approves.
The store built during setup is the **same store** that will later take real sales, not a separate test site. Only the content differs, because no suppliers or real products exist yet.

Before suppliers are contacted, **fill** the store with demo products instead of real supplier products. The store should look as it will when it sells, so suppliers can picture their own products on it.
Examples: ShakaSurfboards.com (surf niche) and Happy Paws (pet supply niche) are demo stores built to a supplier-ready standard. A niche is one specific product category.
Both are **design showcases** that resemble a real store.
A supplier-facing store should look **exactly like** a live store. The only difference is that the products are demo items. It must not look half-built.
Suppliers review the store before approval, so it should **look complete** even with only a few products. It should show what the store will look like once the supplier's products are uploaded.
Suppliers apply the same doubt a future customer would. A store that looks untrustworthy fails both audiences.
Trust signals (things that make a shop look safe and real) are therefore the **core criteria** (the main tests).
What a supplier-ready demo store is (continued)
Suppliers judge a retailer partly on how the store looks, so store quality matters before the first sale. A **professional look** raises the chance of approval.
The store should be **lean** (small and simple) but credible (believable). Use sample collections (groups of products, like categories) and sample products that match the target niche.
Keep it clean, not a large store with many pages or products.
Build it lean but good-looking, without many extra content pages or a large product upload. Add the extras after **vendor approval**. A vendor is the brand or supplier.
The goal before approval is a credible, functional store, **not a finished one**.
Minimum set for credibility: a working logo, a favicon (small icon in the browser tab), colors, fonts, a single slide (one picture in the homepage slideshow), a few collections,
a pre-footer (signup area above the page bottom) and an email signup.
Postpone (leave for later): announcement bars (thin banners at the top of the page), mega menu details (large drop-down menu settings), blog content, buyer guides
and advanced product card settings (options for the box each product appears in).
The store must look **relevant** to its niche before outreach. Add products from the chosen niche, even placeholders, so the brand sees a store that matches its category.
Use the niche-specific demo products and **stock sources** described below.
Build a **new demo store** for each niche, even if you already own other stores. Mention your existing experience when contacting suppliers, and say the new store goes live on a specific date.
A demo store can **stay small** while suppliers are contacted, for example three collections with three products each. It does not need rebuilding when the niche changes.
**Finish the build first**, to the final look, before contacting suppliers. Then start outreach (contacting suppliers). That way suppliers can picture how their products will appear.
Timing: the store is **built before** suppliers are contacted. Demo products are uploaded so suppliers can review it during approval.
What a supplier-ready demo store is (continued)
Before applying to silver suppliers (a supplier tier), **build the demo store** so the supplier can see a working, professional storefront when it reviews your application.
Have a live, high-quality demo store **before contacting suppliers**, so they can see how their products would look on your site.
Supplier outreach comes **only after** the supplier-ready demo store is complete.
At the demo stage, **no real products** are uploaded and no supplier approval is needed yet. Demo products fill the catalog (the full list of products) so the store looks realistic.
They are replaced by live products when the store goes live.
Loading real products before a supplier has approved you is outside the demo stage. **Use demo products** in the catalog instead.

Store build order, with the product check first:
1. **Build** the store with Elixir (a ready-made Shopify design) by following the step-by-step store build guide.
2. **Optimize** the product page: images, copy (written text), urgency elements (things that push a buyer to act now) and trust badges (small logos that show safety or quality).

3. **Keep** the design clean and trustworthy.
4. **Submit** the store for review via a ticket (a request sent to support) before it goes live.
Conflict on sequencing: one source says not to build a store until a product has been approved. Building early wastes time on products that may not pass review.
Two other sources assume the product choice is already made. They say to build the demo store before supplier outreach.
Applies: **validate** the product first (check it). Once the product line is chosen, build the demo store before contacting suppliers.
Store domain: the store must have its **own domain name** (your own web address). Suppliers see this as a sign of professionalism and an established business.
Shop name and website domain: a Shopify subdomain (a shared address ending in.myshopify.com), such as store-name.myshopify.com, in outreach
or on the store **makes the business look unprofessional** and untrustworthy.

How many demo products (continued)

Across these sources, the figures agree: **stay small**. Five appears most often. 10 to 20 is the upper range.
**Do not overbuild** at this stage.
A demo store needs **about five products** to be credible to suppliers. Product descriptions can be short, because suppliers only need to see what the product pages look like.
Keep the product pages **short** during review. The purpose is to show suppliers how the site is organized, not to impress them with copy.
Collections **do not need** to be filled with products before launch (opening the shop to customers).
**One image** per demo product is sufficient.
p.h: Stock images (ready-made photos you can use): number, sources and legal sourcing: How many images per product

p.t:
Multiple images are not required.
**One product photograph** is sufficient for each demo product.
One image per product at acceptable quality is enough. It **does not need to be perfect**. The best available image is sufficient.

Demo products that have only one product photo are **fine**. Stock images with only one angle are acceptable.
Recommended: **at least one** product photo without people.
Lifestyle photos (photos showing the product in use) with people are optional.
If none is available on Canva (an online design tool), search Google for royalty-free images (usable without paying per use). Get **one product shot** per product.
**Five to 10 images** in total are enough for five demo products plus a homepage banner.

For a mock store (a practice store), use **three to five** royalty-free stock images found through a Google image search.
Do **not use** the supplier images you plan to show in outreach.

**Five distinct product photos** are enough to start. Search the niche plus the words white background.
A **handful** of product photos can be enough at launch.
Only a **handful** of images per product type is needed, because dummy products are removed as soon as real suppliers are live.
Upload **no more than two** source images per product when copying from a source page. If the source page has only one image, upload only that one.
**Never launch** with only demo or stock images. Use stock photos during the build and demo phase. Replace them with supplier product photos as soon as a supplier is approved.
Image sources
**Burst (Shopify's free photo library), Pexels, Pixabay, Negative Space, FreePik, Vex, Adobe (free section), FreeImages.com, Unsplash**

Notes: Free stock photo sites
**Burst, Pexels, Negative Space, Freepik, Vecteezy, Adobe Stock, Canva with Magic Media (AI-generated)**

Notes: Use when supplier images are unavailable or you need more visual variations
**123RF.com**

Notes: Millions of images, $2 to $3 per photo. Use when supplier images are unavailable. Older (2021).
**Paid stock photos, about $1 per image**

Notes: Paid sites can fill gaps when free royalty-free images are scarce. Older (2021).
**Paid stock photos, a dollar or two each**

Notes: Buy a few only if free images cannot be found. Older (2021).
**Canva Magic Media (an AI image maker inside Canva) and licensed stock**

Notes: Shows the layout of a product page without implying an existing supplier relationship
**Pexels**

Notes: Free stock site with a product-type search, useful for placeholders. Older (2019).
**Pixabay**
Notes: Free stock alternative

Ids: ,
**Pexels, Pixabay, Google Images, Alibaba, AliExpress**
Notes: Search for usable photos. If nothing usable turns up, search for a very similar product and use its photos.
**Instagram hashtags (customer-style UGC, user-generated content, meaning photos made by customers)**

Notes: One weighted hula hoop campaign using such images reached an 8 to 9 percent conversion rate.
**Fiverr (an online freelancer marketplace)**
Notes: About 5 to 10 USD to fix backgrounds and make the product stand out, or retouch with an AI image tool when photos are pixelated or cluttered
**Brand public sites**
Notes: if no suitable stock photos exist, use photos from brands you have not contacted yet, for example from their public sites. Replace them once the supplier is approved.
Paid stock photos are generally **not worth buying** for a demo or mock store. If images have already been bought, reuse them on other content pages and in social media marketing. Older (2019).
Google Images, Pinterest and similar sites are **not a stock source** for this purpose. Use the sources in the table above. (Conflict noted below.)
Sourcing procedures

Procedure: Commercial rights on Google Images
1. **Search** your niche on google.com/images.

2. Click Tools.
3. Click Usage Rights.
4. Select 'Commercial and other licenses'.

5. Review results and **verify** each image by visiting its source site before using.
Procedure: Labeled for reuse on Google Images

1. **Open** Google and search for the product type, for example leather sofa.
2. Click Images.
3. Click Tools.

4. Open the usage rights menu and select **Labeled for reuse**.
5. Save **only a handful** of images for the demo products.
Procedure: Labeled for reuse, from a store guide

1. **Search** the product type on Google.
2. Switch to the Images tab.
3. Open Tools.

4. **Set** Usage rights to 'Labeled for reuse'. Downloaded images are then royalty-free and safe to use on a website.
Setting: Google Images path for royalty-free photos

Google search > Images tab > Tools > Usage rights > **'Labeled for reuse'**.
'Labeled for reuse with modification' is the alternative when edits are planned.

Procedure: Royalty-free images for demo products, older (2020)
1. **Search** Google for the product name, for example leather sofa.

2. Click Images.
3. Click Tools.
4. Click Usage rights.

5. **Choose** labeled for reuse or labeled for reuse with modification.
6. **Download** a set of images and name the products as you want.

7. **Write** a one or two sentence basic description for each product.
**Free stock photo sites** can also be used.

Procedure: Free images for demo products, older (2021)
1. **Search** Google Images for the product name.

2. Click Tools, then choose Usage rights and **select** a free-to-use option.
3. **Pick** suitable stock images to use as demo products.
4. Alternatively, **browse** Pixabay (a free stock photo site) for free stock images.
Sourcing procedures (continued)

5. **Upload** 5 to 10 demo products and replace them with real products once suppliers are approved.
Procedure: Free images with usage rights, older (2021)

1. **Run** a Google image search for your product.
2. Open Tools.

3. Under Usage rights, **select** Creative Commons licenses (licenses that allow free sharing).
4. **Use** the results that show the product clearly.

Pixabay is a **free stock photo alternative**.
Procedure: Demo product pages, older (2018)
1. **Open** Google Images and search for the product, for example stand-up paddle boards.

2. Click the Images tab, then Tools, then Usage rights, and **choose** Labeled for reuse.
3. **Select** a royalty-free image of the product.

4. **Create** a product page named after the product, for example orange paddle board.
5. **Add** a few lines describing the product, such as size, color, brand, and included parts.
Setting, older (2018): Google Images > Settings > Advanced search > Usage rights dropdown > **Free to use or share** > Advanced search.

Choose images labeled for reuse and use them **only as placeholders** until supplier images arrive.
**Do not copy** images from other sites.
Setting, older (2019): Google Images > Tools > Usage rights > **Labeled for reuse**. Use this filter to find product photos you can legally use as stock images for a demo store.
Setting, older (2019): To find demo product images, **search** the product term in Google, open the Images tab, click Tools, then set Usage rights to 'Labeled for reuse'.

Use the generic photos you find for your demo store.
Procedure, older (2020): Image sourcing for a new store before brands send photos
1. **Start** with stock photo sites, since only a handful of images per product is needed.
2. If no suitable stock photos exist, **use** photos from brands you have not contacted yet, for example from their public sites.
3. **Replace** these placeholders with supplier images once the supplier is approved.

Images labeled for reuse **can be published** on your own website without the risk of a copyright claim (a legal demand from the owner).
Google Images labeled 'licensable' means the copyright holder (the legal owner) **expects payment**.
**Always verify** the source website to confirm the actual licensing terms (the exact rules for use) before using any image found through the commercial license filter.
**Do not copy** product photos from competitor websites. Use free stock sites to avoid legal risks and to demonstrate professionalism.
**Do not copy** product photos from Google Shopping (Google's product search) or competitor sites. Use your own photos or licensed stock images to avoid rights problems.

**Do not copy** images from other sites.
**Do not use** actual supplier photos or PLR (Private Label Rights, content sold for rebranding).
**Never upload** real supplier products, photos or descriptions before you have approval.
If you use royalty-free stock photos from image search, you **can keep them** on a demo store.
Legal rules for images (continued)
If the rights are unclear, **remove them** and use images from suppliers that have approved you.
Demo products that use another supplier's photos should be **deleted** once that supplier approves.
Demo product pages should show only a general idea of a future product page. They **must not** be used to claim that a brand has already approved the store.
Using a supplier's photos for demo products before approval **usually does no harm**. Stock photos avoid the question entirely and are easy to swap out. (Conflict noted below.)
Conflict on supplier photos: (2019) says supplier photos usually do no harm. (2020), and say not to use them before approval.
Applies: use **royalty-free or licensed images** before approval. is older advice.
Conflict on competitor copying: the competitor-copy procedure in includes copying images from the source page. and forbid copying competitor photos.
Applies: **copy only the title and description** where allowed. Replace photos with licensed or own images.
Demo store images **do not need top quality**. A demo store shows the setup, not conversion (the share of visitors who buy). Focus on **consistent sizing**.

Canva procedure, older (2024)
1. Click **Create a design** in the top right.
2. Choose **Custom size**.

3. Enter **600 x 600 pixels** and click Create new design.
4. Add images with Magic Media (AI generated) or drag in your own.
5. Save; all images have the same size.

Demo-site images can stay in place during setup. After launch and once suppliers are onboard (signed up and set up with you), **swap them** for supplier and brand lifestyle images that show the actual products.
Demo product content: Descriptions
Demo product descriptions can be **identical across products**.
Use a generic template (a fill-in layout) with placeholders (blank spots) swapped out for each product. Do not overthink the creation process.
Demo product example: name Aloha Blue Longboard Surfboard, weight **13 pounds**, with description, key features, and specifications filled in from a provided template.
**Do not use Lorem Ipsum** (dummy filler text) for product descriptions on demo stores. Write basic but genuine sentences describing actual product attributes and benefits. Older (2020).
Older (2020) **example sentence**, given in italics: This blue eight-foot surfboard accommodates up to 150 pounds and is great for enjoying water activities during favorable weather.
Demo product descriptions can be **basic placeholders**. They do not need persuasive copy (sales-focused writing) at the supplier-approval stage.
A **one- to two-line** description lets the supplier picture its product on the site. Do not optimize for sales or conversions. Older (2018).
Demo products **do not need** materials, dimensions, technical specifications, or detailed descriptions, since customers cannot buy them. Generic product descriptions are sufficient. Older (2020).
Mock product descriptions and images can be taken from images **labeled for reuse** in Google image search, combined with basic descriptions. Older (2020).
Supplier product descriptions may be used for demo or test products **only if** they come directly from the brand.
**Search a sentence** from the description in Google. If it appears on many sites, it is the brand's stock text (text many sites reuse). Older (2019).
Copying a description that someone else rewrote or paid for, to make it look unique, **creates a copyright problem**. Write your own description, or use the brand's original text. Older (2019).
**Do not present** a demo product as stock you are selling, and do not write a long invented story about it. The demo page only shows suppliers how their product could look on the site. Older (2018).
Rich text (formatted text blocks) is not needed for supplier approval and **can be hidden**.
Turn it on later for brand story or promotion content once the store is live and the unique value proposition (what makes you different) is clear.
Product reviews, vendor names and secondary images need product data that a demo store does not have yet. **Leave those options off** until the store has the content.
Names, prices and vendor

Name pattern: **size, product type and color**. Example: a clear, descriptive title. Older (2018).
Example: seven foot blue standup paddle board.
Demo products **do not need invented brand names** or elaborate descriptions. The brand name can be the store name. Older (2021).
**Do not invent** a company or brand name that does not match the picture. Older (2019).
Demo products may have **made-up names** and invented prices, since they are placeholders and not meant to be sold.
Demo products should be **generic items** from the same category as the niche. For example, a lamp or candlestick for a chandelier store.

This lets a supplier see what the catalog page for that category would look like.
Price: use **$799** for demo products.

Price: the price **can be anything**. Image size or editing does not matter, because demo products will be deleted later.
Price: the exact price is **not critical** for demos.
**Show average prices** and generic inventory numbers (stock counts) on the demo store before launch. Cart (shopping basket) is disabled, so no purchases occur. Older (2022).
**Hide** discount codes and inventory levels, so suppliers do not see broken or unfinished elements. (Conflict noted below.)

Vendor for a demo: **your store name**.
Vendor for a demo: **your own company name**, since it does not matter for demonstration.
Supplier name field: enter **your own store name** instead of a real supplier's name. Older (2019).
Conflict on displayed prices and inventory: (2022) says show average prices and generic inventory numbers. says hide inventory levels and discount codes.

Applies: **show** plausible generic figures if you want the catalog to look realistic.
Applies: **hide** them if the goal is to keep the page free of unfinished elements.
**Do not feature** products from brands you are not yet authorized to sell. Add products to the live store only after the supplier has approved you.
Demo products are temporary placeholders, **removed and replaced** with real supplier products once you have brand partnerships.
AI-assisted content workflow
Full prompt texts are not included in this handbook. Only the opening lines are given, in italics.
Procedure: Demo product with AI prompts
1. **Retrieve** the image prompt that begins You are a professional e-commerce product photographer. Customize it by inserting your product name (for example, Blue Surfboard).
Generate the image using Gemini (Google's AI tool) or another AI image generator, then download it.
2. **Obtain** the description prompt starting with You are a professional e-commerce copywriter.
Enter it into ChatGPT (an AI writing tool) or your preferred AI tool, and attach the generated product image so the AI can observe realistic details before writing.

3. **Copy** the resulting product description.
4. **Log into** Shopify admin (the back office where you manage the shop), go to Products, and click Add product.

5. **Enter** your product name in the Title field.
6. **Paste** the AI description into the description editor, and use Preview (view the page before publishing) to check formatting.
7. If bullets are misaligned, select the bulleted text, remove bullets, **reapply** them, and preview again.

8. **Upload** the generated image into product media (the product photo area). One image is sufficient for demos.
9. **Select** an appropriate category (such as Surfboards).

10. **Set** a demo price. The exact price is not critical for demos.
11. **Specify** the product type (such as Surfboards).
12. **Add the tag** (a label on the product) that connects to your automated collections (collections that fill themselves using tags) so the product is positioned correctly.
13. **Save** the product and preview it to confirm the formatting is correct.

14. Repeat this entire workflow (steps 1 to 21) until you have created **10 to 20** demo products.
Procedure: 32-step product workflow
AI-assisted content workflow (continued)

**Access** gemini.google.com, click Create Image, paste the complete Source A Image Prompt that starts with You are a professional e-commerce product photographer creating images for a premium Shopify
store, replace product name goes here with your product, and download the result.

2. **Enter ChatGPT** with the full Demo Product Description Prompt beginning with You are a professional e-commerce copywriter specializing in high conversion Shopify product pages for premium products.
Use Add photos and files to attach your Gemini image, and submit.

3. **Open** Shopify Admin and navigate to Products. Click the Add product button in the top right corner.
4. **Insert** your product name in the Product Title field.
5. **Paste** your ChatGPT description in the Description field through the WYSIWYG editor (a text editor that shows formatting as you type), and click Save.
6. **Preview** the page and look for formatting problems such as misaligned bullet points.
If you find any, go back to the editor, select the affected text, remove the formatting, reapply it, save, and preview again until the formatting is correct.

7. **Set** the Gemini image as the main product image.
8. **Fill** the Product Category field.
9. **Set the Price field to $799**.

10. **Set** the Product Type field to match your category.
11. In the Collections section, **select** your tag-based automated collection.

12. **Save** the product, and review your final product page with a preview.
13. Repeat all preceding steps **10 to 20 times** across your product range.
Example: a completed demo product with title **Aquila Coastline Longboard**, price $799, category surfboards, one AI-generated image, a professional description generated by ChatGPT,
and collection assignment through tags.
Shopify is the online shop software you use to build your store. A demo product is a sample item.
p.h: Setting up demo products in Shopify

p.t: You use it to show suppliers how their products will look. It is not for sale.
Upload procedure

Procedure: Uploading a demo product to Shopify
1. Go to **Products**, then click Add products.

2. Enter the product title (the name).
3. Paste the product description from the template (a ready-made text) and change it to fit.

4. Select the product category from the dropdown (a list you open with a click).
5. Enter the product type (a label that groups similar products).
6. Enter the vendor (the brand or seller name). Your store name is fine for demos.
7. Add tags (short labels). Tags fill collections automatically. A collection is a group of products shown together.
8. Drag the product image into the media section (the photo area).
9. Enter the **selling price**, the compare-at price (the old price, shown crossed out), and the cost per item (what you pay).
10. Leave inventory tracking unchecked. Inventory means your stock count. Only check it if you track stock.

11. Enter the SKU if provided. A SKU is your own stock code for the item.
12. Enter the product weight.

13. Skip variants for demos. Variants are versions of one product, such as sizes or colours.
14. Click **Save**.
Procedure: Competitor-copy route, Source B A competitor is another shop that sells similar products.

1. Open the source product page (the original product page) on the competitor site.
2. Copy the title and paste it into the Title field in Shopify.
3. Copy the description and specifications and paste them into the Description field.

4. Save the source images, using **no more than two** per product. Upload them with Add file under Media.
5. Enter the price, and optionally the compare-at price.
6. Set the product type, vendor, tags and status. Tick Online Store.
7. Set the quantity. Tick the physical product box (a physical product is an item you ship), then **save**.
Conflict: this route copies images from a competitor. and forbid this. See the legal rules above.
Settings reference

**Product status**
Where: Product editor
Demo rule: Set to **Active to show the product on the storefront (the public shop pages). Draft** hides it from all sales channels (the places you sell). New products are created as Draft by default.

**Online Store**
Where: Sales channels and apps

Demo rule: Must be ticked. Without it, an Active product still does not appear on the front end (the page customers see).
**Product type**
Where: Organization section
Demo rule: Use the name of the collection the product belongs to, for example Solar Power. It must match the collection so the product is grouped correctly.

**Vendor**
Where: Organization section
Demo rule: Your own company name is fine for demos.
**Tags**

Where: Organization section
Demo rule: Several tags per product are allowed. The tag must match the collection name, for example solar.
**Price**

Where: Pricing
Demo rule: The price customers see.
**Compare at price**
Where: Pricing

Demo rule: The original price, shown struck through next to the sale price. Enter a **higher** value here than in Price to display a sale. Example: Price A$ 2,350.00 with Compare at price A$ 2,450.00.

**Charge tax on this product**
Where: Pricing
Demo rule: Tick if you need to charge tax in your country. For demos, tax can be left for later.

**Track quantity and Available quantity**
Where: Inventory

Demo rule: Tick Track quantity and set Available quantity **above zero**, for example 10. At zero, Shopify shows the product as out of stock.
Ids: ,

**SKU and Barcode**
Where: Inventory
Demo rule: Can be left empty for demos. Enter SKU if provided.

Ids: ,
**This is a physical product**
Where: Shipping
Demo rule: Tick it. Weight, customs information and HS code can be skipped for demos. An HS code is an international product code used at customs (the border office).

**Media**
Where: Media section
Demo rule: Add file from the computer or Add media from URL. In a browser, right-click a source image to use Save Image As or Copy Image Address.

**Template suffix**
Where: Theme templates
Demo rule: The default product template can be left unchanged while the first demo products are uploaded.
Mistakes and checks
A product with status **Draft is not shown on the storefront. A product with Active status but without the Online Store box ticked is not shown either.**
**Check both** before expecting a product to appear.
A product with a quantity of **zero** and tracking on displays as out of stock. Always set a quantity when Track quantity is ticked.
Use **Preview** in Shopify to see how a saved product appears on the site. Before the site is designed, the page can look unfinished. The preview still confirms that the product data has loaded.
**Do not** assign demo products to collections by hand. Use the automated, tag-based collections (collections that fill themselves from tags) created earlier in store setup.
Time: four products took about **10 minutes**.
A theme is the design package of your store. The theme editor is where you change its look.
**Skip** customizing pages and blog templates in the Shopify theme editor. A blog is a news or article section. This can wait until the store is live and needs more individual content.
For a basic demo store, only the sticky content and media settings in the Product information section need changes. Sticky content stays on screen while the visitor scrolls.
The other settings can stay at their defaults until the store is ready for live products.
Hide promotional elements and coupons. Promotional elements are ads or sale banners. Coupons are discount codes.
Keep product pages clean and simple, with a professional layout, clean navigation and functional pages.
Hide features that are not yet needed, such as discount codes and inventory levels. At the demo stage, **all links should work** and every function should behave correctly.
Minimum theme elements: see the minimum set in the first section.
**Postpone** these: announcement bars (thin banners at the top of the page), mega menu details (large dropdown menus) and advanced product card settings (the box showing one product in a list).
Pre-launch checklist before supplier outreach
Outreach means contacting suppliers. A supplier is a company that makes or sells the products you resell.
Procedure: Supplier-ready store checklist, in order
1. **Buy a domain name** in Shopify and connect it to the store. A domain name is your web address, for example yourstore.com.
2. Remove the demo-store notification bar at the top of the site. This is the bar that says it is a demo.
3. Keep the product count small. **Three to five** demo products is enough. More is unnecessary.
4. Replace every generic or fake phone number with a real phone number, or remove the phone number entirely.
5. Delete unneeded default content, such as the empty blog that Shopify creates. A blog is not required when contacting suppliers.
6. Open the About Us, Shipping and Guarantee (guarantee/returns) pages. Fill in all text so it reads complete, and **click every link** to confirm it works.

7. Click through the site the way a supplier would. Check that it looks presentable and finished.
Procedure: Pre-outreach check, 2023
1. Is live at your final domain, not Shopify's default URL (the free web address Shopify gives you).
2. Has all internal links working. Internal links are links between your own pages.
3. Does not contain broken pages or placeholder content. Broken pages show an error. Placeholder content is fill-in text that is not final.
4. Has social media links pointing to actual accounts, not default Shopify links.

5. Looks complete and professional, as suppliers judge your credibility by the quality of the site.
Procedure: Pre-outreach check, 2023

1. Attach your **own domain name**, not a myshopify.com address.
2. Remove all blank image placeholders (empty picture boxes).
3. Make sure the contact page has a working contact form (a form visitors fill in to send you a message).

4. Five to 10 products is enough, and checkout does not need to be enabled. Checkout is the step where customers pay.
5. Remove the store password.
Rules for the checklist:
Pre-launch checklist before supplier outreach (continued)
Your store must have its **own domain name**.
**Display** an actual phone number prominently. Suppliers see a real, reachable phone number as proof that you run a legitimate, accountable business.
Replace the generic phone number with a real one, or remove it entirely.
**All links** on the store must work. Broken links suggest neglect and weaken supplier confidence.
The store should look presentable and appear exactly as it will when the site goes live. **Do not show it** to suppliers while it is under construction or contains placeholder content.
Pre-launch quality: it must look like a real, working store, with no test pages, no dead links and no spelling errors. It must be trustworthy enough that a customer would buy from it.
Before calling suppliers, **add a price guarantee page and a privacy policy page (a page explaining how you handle customer data).**
**This takes about 15 to 20 minutes** using ready-made scripts (ready-made texts) or a generator (a tool that writes the text for you). Older (2019).
Fill the About Us page and the shipping and returns policy page.
Mistakes that signal the store is not real: a demo-store notification bar, a generic fake phone number, or unfinished default pages such as a placeholder blog.
Mistake: using a Shopify subdomain, such as store-name.myshopify.com, in outreach or on the live store. A subdomain is a free address under Shopify's name.

Costs for the checklist items: a domain name costs between **5 and 20 USD**.
Build-before-contact procedure, Source B
1. Set up the store on Shopify. Shopify hosts the store (keeps it online) on its own software, so no custom platform is needed.
2. Add branding, a logo and basic design, so the site looks like a real e-commerce store. Branding means your name, logo, colours and look. E-commerce means selling online.
3. Make it a demo website. It does not have to be 100 percent complete, but it must look solid when you show it to suppliers.
4. Use the demo site when you contact suppliers to show that the business is serious.
5. After approval, upload the supplier's products with their data, pricing and images. Then optimize (improve) the products and the website.
Password and sales during the demo stage: Remove the storefront password
The storefront is the public shop side that customers see.
The storefront password is a lock page that hides the store from visitors.
A new Shopify store is password-protected by default. **Remove the password** in the Online Store preferences before suppliers review the store.
**Remove the Shopify storefront password** before contacting suppliers. A live store, which is online and open to visitors, makes the business look real and saves suppliers an extra step.
**Keep the store password off** during supplier onboarding. Onboarding means signing suppliers up.
Suppliers and pending suppliers (suppliers waiting for approval) often check the site, and a password blocks them.

A store with the password page still on looks unfinished to suppliers who visit the URL (web address). **Disable the password** before sending the URL. The store can be live but not promoted at this stage.
There are no ads or search visibility (showing up in Google) yet, and checkout is not connected.
The store can be made live with demo products before real products are uploaded.

Nobody will find it without marketing (advertising and promotion), and checkout is not connected, so no one can buy the demo products. **Connect checkout only after** real supplier products are uploaded.
Demo products are only for showing suppliers how their products will look. They are never sold or marketed. They must be **deleted** from the account before the store goes live to customers.

Demo products left live can be pulled into the product feed (the product list sent to shopping sites), cause feed errors, and let customers check out for items you cannot sell. **Delete all demo products** before launch.
Shopify payment setting: go to **Settings > Payments** and disable all payment options so no customer can buy.
Alternatively, go to Settings > Shipping and delivery and select no shipping zones (the countries or areas you ship to), so no shipping option can be chosen.
To stop the store from taking orders, leave every payment method inactive so checkout cannot be completed. Or set the inventory of the products to **zero**. Older (2021).
Keep real sales off (continued)
**Turn off** or leave unlinked the payment gateways in the Shopify admin (the back office where you manage the store), so no real orders can be placed.
A payment gateway is the link to the service that takes card payments. Older (2019).
A payment processor (the service that handles card payments) **does not need** to be set up before supplier calls, because no sales are being taken yet. Older (2019).
Conflict on zero inventory: says set quantity above zero for demo products, because zero shows the product as out of stock. says set inventory to zero to stop orders.
Applies: keep quantity above zero when the product should show as available. Use zero or inactive payments when orders must be blocked.

Procedure: Launch the store before suppliers are ready, 2025
1. Remove password from store (make it accessible).

2. Disable all payment methods so customers cannot complete purchases.
3. Add demo products to show to potential suppliers.

4. Keep demo products for the first week while contacting suppliers.
5. Once the first supplier is approved, upload their products.

6. Remove demo products.
7. Continue adding supplier products.

Procedure: After the first supplier approves, 2021
1. Remove the demo products.
p.h: Replacing demo products after supplier approval

p.t:
2. Upload that supplier's live products.
3. Keep adding products as further suppliers are approved.
Procedure: Replacement, 2019
1. Before supplier approval, upload about 4 to 5 demo products using stock images (ready-made photos from a photo library).

2. Get approved with real suppliers.
3. Upload the real supplier products.
4. Remove the demo products.

Rules:
**Remove** the test or dummy products (fake items used for trials) once the first real supplier is approved and its products are uploaded.
**Remove** the demo products as soon as real products from an approved supplier are uploaded.
Replacing demo products after supplier approval (continued)
Demo products are removed and replaced with real supplier products once brand partnerships (agreements with brands) are established.
**Remove** the placeholder products as soon as the first real supplier approves. Older (2020).
Before contacting a supplier, **leave** the demo products on the store, so the supplier can see how its items would look.
Remove only a specific supplier's real products before contacting that same supplier, so the store does not look already approved. Older (2019).
**Replace** demo products with real products from approved suppliers as soon as they are approved. Demo products that use another supplier's photos should be deleted once that supplier approves.

Older (2021).
A demo store can be used for real products by **deleting** the demo products and uploading the real ones. Older (2022).
**Replace** the stock images with actual supplier product photos immediately upon supplier approval.
Replace demo images with real supplier images after the first approval.
After launch and once suppliers are onboard, **swap** demo images for supplier and brand lifestyle images (photos showing the product in use) that show the actual products.
Source B's build route: after approval, upload the supplier's products with their data, pricing and images, then optimize.
Once a supplier is approved, the store **continues** with its products. A small store does not need rebuilding when the niche (the market you focus on) changes.
**Build a new demo store** for each niche, rather than reusing the store for a different niche.
**Do not** feature products from unauthorized brands (brands that have not given permission) on the live store.
Demo products are placeholders. **Delete them** before the store goes live. Do not leave demo products live.
A done-for-you service means someone else builds the store for you, for a fee.
Two routes to a supplier-ready demo store
There are two routes. You can build the demo store yourself, step by step.
Or you can outsource the web design (have someone else design it) to a done-for-you service. The done-for-you service delivers a finished store that the buyer owns **100 percent**.
The done-for-you web design service is a **paid upgrade**. Buyers who already bought it submit the web design form.
Buyers who have not bought it can sign up through an information form to add it to their account.
Choosing the done-for-you service lets you **skip** the self-build steps for the demo store and move straight to contacting suppliers.
Choosing to build it yourself means working through every design step first. Supplier outreach starts only after that step is complete.
The Ultimate Upgrade done-for-you store includes professional setup of these accounts: Google Search Console (a Google tool showing how Google sees your site),
Google Merchant Center (a Google tool that lists your products), Google Analytics (visitor tracking), and Google Ads (paid advertising). The standard done-for-you store does not include these setups.
A custom store build has typically taken **three to five business days**. Reply to the delivery email with any edit requests, since most owners are satisfied on day one.

**Time**
Build yourself: An experienced builder can set up a demo Shopify store in **under 24 hours**. A first-time builder may need a few days.

Done-for-you: A custom store build has typically taken three to five business days.
**Your work**

Build yourself: Work through every design step, then start supplier outreach.
Done-for-you: **Skip** the self-build steps and move straight to outreach.
**Cost**
Build yourself: A domain name costs 5 to 20 USD. Initial branding, such as a logo from a freelance platform like Fiverr (a site where freelancers sell their work), can cost about 20 to 30 USD.

Done-for-you: A paid upgrade. Buyers who have not purchased it sign up through an information form.
**Ownership**

Build yourself: Your own store on Shopify.
Done-for-you: The buyer owns the finished store 100 percent.
Building custom e-commerce software instead would cost **tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars**. Shopify avoids this cost.
The build-yourself route is described in the build-before-contact procedure above.
The build should be done on Shopify, and then shown to suppliers.
Website checks before supplier outreach: What the store must look like before suppliers see it
The store must look complete before suppliers see it.
That means no placeholder phone numbers or emails, no filler or instructional text, and **every link must work**.
Real phone numbers and emails are **not required yet**. They are added before contacting suppliers.
Store branding (colors, color scheme, business name) must be configured in Shopify before any supplier contact. **Finish branding first** so the store can be shown as complete.
1. Open your store and go through every page.
Look for typos, broken links, placeholder phone numbers or emails, and filler text such as instructional placeholder sentences.
2. **Click every link** on the store and confirm each one works as intended.

3. Send the store link to a friend or family member. Ask them to browse, and collect any feedback on things you missed.
4. **Fix** everything they flag, so the site looks complete.
5. In Shopify Admin, go to **Online Store > Themes** and click Remove Password, so the store is publicly reachable.
After long work on a store, the builder tends to overlook obvious errors.
p.h: Why an outside tester is needed

p.t: An outside person testing the site with fresh eyes helps catch them.

**Where**: Shopify Admin > Online Store > Themes
**Action**: Click **Remove Password**
p.h: Password removal: Making the store publicly visible

p.t: **Result**: Anyone who types the domain name can reach the store
To make the store publicly visible in Shopify, go to **Online Store > Themes** in Shopify Admin and click Remove Password. Once removed, anyone who types the domain name can reach the store.
A store still locked behind the Shopify password page cannot be shown to potential suppliers. So **remove the password** before supplier outreach begins.
Demo stores only need to look realistic for a supplier review. They do not need to prove access to the products.
Products can use free stock images and simple descriptions.
Before suppliers approve you, you can upload placeholder products with royalty-free images (images you can use without paying each time) found through Google image search.

This lets you preview the store. If a supplier asks, explain that the store is being built and the placeholder products are **not for sale**. This matches your message that you are launching a new store.
